Q: Can you tell me a bit about where you grew up?

A: Oh, it was a very small place. You wouldn't know it. A townland outside Strokestown — just fields and bogs and the one road into town. We had no electricity until I was about nine or ten, and even then it was only the one bulb in the kitchen. My mother used to say we were rich in fresh air and poor in everything else. [laughs] She wasn't wrong.

Q: What was your family like?

A: There were seven of us children. I was the fourth. My father was a quiet man — a farmer, never said much, but you always knew where you stood with him. My mother was the opposite, always talking, always singing. She had a song for everything. I can still hear her at the sink. I couldn't tell you the half the words now but the tunes are all still there.

Q: What made you decide to leave Ireland?

A: Decide is a strong word. [pause] There wasn't much to stay for, if I'm honest. My two older brothers had already gone — one to England, one to America. There was no work. The farm couldn't support all of us. My friend Attracta said she was going to Birmingham and did I want to come, and I said yes almost before she'd finished the sentence. I was nineteen. I thought it was a great adventure. I didn't think about what I was leaving.

Q: What was it like when you first arrived in Birmingham?

A: Cold. [laughs] And grey. Everything was grey. The buildings, the sky, the people's coats. At home you had all that green and here it was just brick and chimney smoke. We had a room in a house in Erdington — four Irish girls in one room, which sounds terrible but actually it was great fun. We were young and we were all in the same boat. The landlady was a Mrs. Horton and she did not care for the Irish one bit, but she took our money all the same.

Q: How did you end up becoming a nurse?

A: That was Attracta's idea as well. She said the hospitals were taking on Irish girls and the pay was decent and you got accommodation. I'd never thought about nursing particularly. I'd thought about — I don't know, I had some vague idea about working in a shop, something like that. But nursing turned out to suit me down to the ground. I liked having something useful to do with my hands. I liked that you could see when you'd helped someone.

Q: Can you tell me about meeting your husband?

A: [smiles] Dermot. He was from Galway. I met him at a dance in the Irish Centre in 1965 — he stood on my foot and then apologised for about ten minutes without stopping. I thought, this man is harmless enough, I'll dance with him again. We were married two years later. He was a good man. Very funny, quietly. You had to listen or you'd miss it.

Q: Is there anything you wish you'd asked your own parents, before they were gone?

A: [long pause] Yes. I wish I'd asked my mother about her own life before she had us. Who she was before she was our mother. You don't think to ask when you're young — they're just your parents, they've always been there. And then they're not, and all those years are just gone. That's the thing, isn't it. You think there'll be more time.
